title: I want to leave but I'm scared of what comes after
summary: Scared to leave but not sure if the fear means stay or go? How to tell whether you're staying for the relationship or from the alternative.
body_markdown:
You have run the conversation in your head a hundred times. You know how you would start it. You also know exactly what comes after: finding somewhere to live, money that does not stretch across two households, the kids asking why, the friends who will quietly pick a side, a birthday next year where the phone does not ring. So you stay another week. Then another. Then it is a year later and you are still lying awake at 2am doing the same math.


The fear is not irrational, and that is the first thing worth saying, because most advice treats it as a hurdle to be talked out of. Leaving a long relationship is genuinely expensive. Money, time, housing, the whole daily infrastructure of a life you built with another person. Being scared of that is not weakness. It is accurate.


But accurate is not the same as decisive. Here is the part nobody says plainly enough: **fear of what comes after is not evidence that you should stay, and it is not evidence that you should go.** It is information about the price of one option. Price is real. Price is not an answer.


If your feed served you the divorce before-and-after photos this year, the ones where someone looks ten years younger six months out, notice what those clips leave out. You only ever see the after. Nobody films the eighteen months of lying awake deciding, and nobody films the couples who stayed and rebuilt something real either. The feed has a direction. Your actual life does not have to go the same way.


## Staying for it, or staying from it


This is the distinction that tends to move people, and it is not the same as asking whether you still love them.


Staying *for* the relationship means there is something in it you still want. Maybe not today's version of it, but a version you can describe: how they are with your mother, the way you two handle a crisis, something you are still trying to get back to. You could finish the sentence "I'm staying because ______" with something that has a person in it.


Staying *from* the alternative means the sentence finishes with a consequence instead. I'm staying because I can't afford to go. Because I'd have to tell my parents. Because I'd be starting over at forty-three. Every one of those may be true. But notice that none of them are about your partner at all. You could swap in almost any partner and the sentence would still work.


Most people are doing some of both, and that is normal. The question is the ratio, and whether it has been sliding in one direction for years.


## What people actually describe when they say they're scared


In Maia conversations, the tell is usually the order things come out.


People open with the spreadsheet. Rent in the next town over, whose name is on the car, what the custody schedule would probably look like, how long the savings would last. It is detailed. It has clearly been rehearsed for a long time. Then, somewhere much later and almost as an aside, comes one flat little sentence about the relationship itself. *I just don't think I'm happy.* That is it. That is the whole case, and it gets about eight words.


The fear is loud and specific. The wanting is quiet and vague. That does not mean the wanting is smaller. It means it has had far less practice being said out loud, usually because saying it out loud has consequences and the spreadsheet does not.


So if you have been treating the vagueness as proof you do not have a real reason, consider that you may just be out of practice at the other half of the conversation.


## Make the fear specific enough to answer


Fear stays enormous while it stays general. "I couldn't manage on my own" is unanswerable. Broken into parts, it usually is not.


- **Write the fears down as separate lines.** Not "everything falls apart." Housing. Income. Childcare. Health insurance. Who I would call on a bad night. They are different problems with different answers, and a couple of them are probably already solved.
- **Mark which are facts and which are forecasts.** "My name is not on the lease" is a fact. "I would never meet anyone again" is a forecast, and you are making it from inside the most depleted year of your life.
- **Get one real number.** Not the catastrophic one in your head. Look up what a one bedroom actually costs where you would go. People are often braced for a figure much worse than the real one, and occasionally the real one is worse, which is also useful to know.
- **Ask what you would tell a friend.** If someone you loved described this exact relationship to you, in these words, what would you say back? Then sit with the fact that you would probably never say to them what you say to yourself.


None of this decides anything. It just shrinks the fear down to something you can look at directly instead of something that runs the whole night.


## The trap of waiting until it's bad enough


The most common way people stay stuck is waiting for permission. Some incident awful enough to justify the decision to everyone, so nobody can ask why you did not try harder.


Two things about that. First, it can wait forever. Plenty of relationships never produce a single event you could name in a sentence, they just quietly cost you more than they give back, year after year. Second, it means you are outsourcing the decision to your partner's worst behavior, which is a strange person to put in charge of your life.


Certainty is the other version of the same trap. You are not going to feel sure. People who leave rarely feel sure, and people who stay and rebuild rarely feel sure either. The question is not whether you can be certain, it is whether the reason you are still here is one you would choose on a day when you were not exhausted. If you cannot tell anymore, that may be its own answer about[whether this is a rough patch or the end](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/should-i-break-up-or-keep-trying) , and it is worth asking whether you have already[stopped recognizing yourself in this](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/ive-lost-myself-in-my-relationship) .


## Waiting is allowed, if you actually choose it


There is a real difference between staying because you have decided to stay for now, and staying because you cannot make yourself move. The first has a shape. You know what you are waiting for, whether that is a lease ending, a job starting, a school year finishing, or one honest attempt at repair you have not made yet. The second is just the days going by.


If you decide to wait, say what you are waiting for and roughly when. Same as anyone weighing[the timing around a holiday or a family milestone](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/break-up-before-the-holidays-or-wait) . A chosen wait is a decision. An indefinite one is the thing that eats years.


And if you are still hoping for repair, be honest about who has been doing the work. If you have been[the only one trying for a long time](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/im-the-only-one-trying-in-my-relationship) , then the question is no longer your technique. It is their willingness.


One more thing, and it matters. If part of what scares you is your partner's reaction, if you are afraid of what they would do, if they control the money or your access to your own family, that is a different situation from the one this page is about, and it needs more than a plan. Please talk to someone you trust, or the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233, before you make a move.


Most people carrying this never say it out loud to anyone, sometimes for years, because saying it makes it real. It can help to talk it through somewhere that has no stake in the outcome and is not going to steer you toward staying or leaving. That is what Maia is for: a place to get the fear out of your head and into words, sort the facts from the forecasts, and find out what you actually think when nobody is waiting for a particular answer.
